utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We shall now continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Djakovic. Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire, did the Court reach any consensus on what you might want to do with my proposal about the illegibles in P1468?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment. Did you not receive an e-mail, Mr. Hannis, asking you to identify the ones you really wanted dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour, and I have a hard copy of the B/C/S where we've highlighted the portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We haven't seen that yet, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I brought it to court, Your Honour, and I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if that can be handed over, we will need to -- and you'll need to intimate it to the other parties. You can pass it round if you like or whatever, but -- and we can get it at the break, but that will have to happen so that if any want to address us on this issue, they can do so, and then we shall decide it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the solemn declaration which you made at the beginning of your evidence that you would tell the truth will continue to apply to your evidence until it's completed. The cross-examination will now continue by Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, General. I wanted to ask you if you had occasion to look at Exhibit P2943, the unsigned statement that was prepared by Philip Coo and others from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first question I want to ask you this morning relates to that, and yesterday at page 21, line 19, Judge Bonomy asked you a question about the Joint Command and the use of that term, and you said, '"Command' pertained to the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps. That is to say that when we talked about the variant as to what we should put in the text, I suggested to him" -- and I think you're talking about General Pavkovic there -- "I suggested to him another variant: Staff of the MUP and the command of the Pristina Corps, and the general said, that's long; how can we put all that down? So then through an exchange of comments, we came to the conclusion, the two of us, that it would be best to put 'Joint Command.'" Do you recall giving that answer yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in 2004 you were asked a similar question, I guess, by Mr. Coo about that, and at paragraph 33 of that statement, you said in 2004, "I remember that at one point I asked General Pavkovic what I should call the document I was keeping notes in. He said, I don't know, but for the time being called it the Joint Command. I remember that in the left corner I wrote 'Joint Command,' the time the meeting started, and the time the meeting ended, and at the outset I listed the people involved." You didn't mention anything about this two-way discussion between the two of you and reaching that consensus. Was your memory better in 2004 about what happened than -- than it is today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are correct. The first statement that I made pertained to the first documents that were written, that is to say before the 22nd of July. As for this here, it's just my interest in respect to the 22nd of July in connection with the notes that I kept. Then I asked again what I should put there in the corner. The General said, put what you've been putting so far, and this so far was on the 6th of July and a few other times when we placed "Joint Command" on a few other documents. So for the most part, this had to do with instructions and general documents of coordination that were there by way of information to the MUP that the army was involved in a certain activity and that they should coordinate their activities with the army. So both are correct. I believe that you have understood what it was that I've been trying to say. These are two different events. Of course, now I'm interpreting them in a different way because the conversations took place in a different way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand what you're saying, but I have a question because I think you maybe -- maybe I interpreted this wrong, but I think you agreed with me that "command" is a word that has a special significance for military men more so than probably for us civilians. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and we discussed a little bit yesterday that when you used the term "Joint Command" for the first time and sent that out to subordinate units, you got some calls back or some contacts from, I think, the 125th and the 549th about what is this Joint Command, right? You have to answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in this discussion, it seems like one reason that you and Pavkovic agreed to use the term "Joint Command" was because it was short rather than writing out Pristina Corps command and command of the staff of the MUP, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you've made the point, and other witnesses have made the point that this Joint Command that included Mr. Sainovic and some of the other civilians who we've mentioned before made a strong point that there was no command authority in that body, right? That it was a coordinating body, if anything. I see Mr. Fila on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things are a problem. First of all, the witness never said that the Joint Command included Sainovic. Please show me where it is that Djakovic, this witness, said that. Other witnesses, too, who said that Sainovic was a member of the Joint Command. Where is that? Tell me. And also, thirdly, where did the witness say that it was a coordinating body? So it's these three things. He didn't say that, either. Then we'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's a basis for inferring the first two, and he definitely said the third one, Mr. Fila. So let's continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do I need to repeat my question, or do you recall it before the intervention?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the question. It is clear to me. I'll answer. There's no need for you to repeat it for me. First of all, it is correct that I did not say that Mr. Sainovic belonged to the command. I certainly did not say that. And secondly, I said that for me the command was the MUP staff and the command of the Pristina Corps throughout. As for Mr. Sainovic and the other gentleman, I saw them there as political organs in charge of certain functions within the republic and the federation. That is how I saw them, and that is how they behaved. I can say with certainty that Mr. Sainovic or Mr. Minic or any one of them never asked me to write something up, to prepare a document, to bring in something to sign. So I do not know of the corps command ever having prepared a single document for Mr. Sainovic, Minic, Matkovic, or any one of them for them to sign and to send to any level of command. That is what I know for sure. As for that part of the corps command, I can be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think you -- you understood me correctly or answered my question, and as far as Mr. Sainovic being a member of the Joint Command, I say that because that exhibit, P1468, the notes of the meetings you took on -- on the first page, the first meeting, he's listed as one of those present, and in later meetings where you list the people present, sometimes you say "All members present," and among those present is Mr. Sainovic. Are you saying he was not a member of that body that met from July to October 1998 in Pristina at those meetings referred to as Joint Command meetings in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying, but what I do claim is that on the occasion of the first meeting no one mentioned the Joint Command, none of the persons present. General Pavkovic, I, no one from the military, no one from the MUP mentioned the Joint Command. None of the civilians mentioned the Joint Command. Even in the text as far as I could see in all the texts, on 150 pages you do not have a single reference to a Joint Command in my notes. That is to say that no one ever at that meeting mentioned the term "Joint Command." Joint Command was an internal fictitious name when there were discussions for the most part between General Pavkovic and myself so that we could separate this and create coordination documents with the MUP because the MUP could not and would not accept a single document where it said "Command of the Pristina Corps." When it said "Joint Command," then the MUP accepted that variant, and that is the only reason. That was the only reason why it said "Joint Command," not because of Mr. Minic or Mr. Sainovic or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, are you certain that there's no mention in your notes of the term "Joint Command" by people attending those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for the title that I wrote myself, this upper part where it said "Joint Command." And I've explained that already, how I put it there and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a look at that in a little bit. But isn't it true that all of those members attending -- at least Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, I'm not sure about Mr. Matkovic, but Mr. Minic and Mr. Sainovic, General Lukic, General Pavkovic eventually all came to refer to that group as the Joint Command, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where was this that Sainovic and Minic called this the Joint Command at these meetings, please? Members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, there's no --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no reason why the question that's been asked cannot be asked. Please confine your -- you know that we fully understand your point on this, but there's no reason why Mr. Hannis cannot try to discover the terms in which these meetings were referred to by the various people who attended them, and there is no doubt Mr. Sainovic was a regular attender. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, let me show you an exhibit that you may or may not have seen before. It's Exhibit P2166, and I can give you a hard copy that may make it easier and quicker. These are -- this is dated the 2nd of November, 1998, described as the "Minutes of the meeting of the operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo at the Beli Dvor palace in Belgrade on 29 October 1998." Have you ever seen this document before now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the content, I'm aware of quite a few of the elements from here, but I haven't seen it in this form. Well, actually, I'm not sure. I know this information, for instance, because I prepared some of this information with the operative organ, what had to do with the combat operations and so on. So I'm aware of some of the data, but whether I actually saw this, well, I know that the meeting was in Belgrade at President Milosevic's. That I know. Now, whether it was on the 2nd of November or -- rather, the 29th of October, right? I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 29th of October according to the minutes. The point I'm trying to get at in connection with this is the use of the term "Joint Command" by Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic, and others. On the first page you'll see the list of all the people attending, and the meeting is chaired by President Milosevic. In the second paragraph, you'll see that Mr. Milosevic opens the sessions and tells who will speak, and he says that General Pavkovic is going to present the proposals of the Joint Command. So apparently, President Milosevic is using the term "Joint Command" in this meeting. Now, if you will go over to page -- let me find it here. Page 9 of the English, and I guess it's page 10 of the B/C/S -- of the B/C/S. I will tell you that this is Mr. Minic speaking. He's been speaking for a couple of pages here. And this has: "In conclusion, Milomir Minic proposed the following." Do you see that? It should be at the very top of your page 10.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 10, you say? Oh, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The very top. "In conclusion, Milomir Minic proposed the following: "The operations staff" -- which is this group meeting on this date -- "should provide an assessment of how successfully the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija has fulfilled the authorisations conferred upon it." So in this meeting with President Milosevic, we see Mr. Minic using the term "Joint Command." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not the one using it. This is a text, a text of the notes taken by -- I mean, General Susic. Now, out of the context of this conversation, how he attributed this to Mr. Minic, well, in some communication he probably had some knowledge that in some discussions the term "Joint Command" was being used, but I'm telling you what I know, and that is that down there in Pristina, it wasn't. I mean, I cannot give you my comments with regard to this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- you were not at this meeting, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And are you saying that Colonel Susic or General Susic made up the term and attributed the use of the words "Joint Command" to Mr. Minic falsely?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's not what I'm saying. Probably like me, the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if somebody in your meeting of the Joint Command in Pristina didn't use the words "Joint Command," you wouldn't put that in your notes, right? You wouldn't make up something to put in the notes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you'll go to page -- I guess it's the bottom of page 13 in the B/C/S and -- the very bottom, and then going on to page 14. It's Mr. Sainovic, Deputy Prime Minister, speaking, and he's described or reported as saying: "Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic agreed with the opinion that the viability of the continued activity of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in its present composition should be re-evaluated." So it appears, according to the notes taken by General Susic, that Mr. Sainovic was using the term "Joint Command" as well. Do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I don't know about these meetings, nor could I have known about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- let me move to another topic related to Joint Command. Yesterday, Judge Bonomy was asking you about certain orders issued in 1999 under the title "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen P1966, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I understand correctly that you were no longer with the Pristina Corps in April or March of 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the territory of Kosovo, though I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see, this is a document that has the heading "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," dated the 22nd of March, 1999, and it's an order to route and destroy the Siptar terrorists in the Malo Kosovo area, and I will tell you this one on the last page has that typewritten word "Joint Command," but there's no handwritten signature by anybody. Is that a practice that you were familiar with, with Joint Command appearing at the top and the bottom of the page with no signature for these orders relating to joint MUP and VJ activity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you next P1967, and I would tell you this one is dated the same day. It also has the words "Joint Command" at the top, and it's described as an amendment to the one that we just looked at, and the numbering system makes it clear that they are related. Now, if we go to that last page of this one, you'll see that this one is actually signed by General Lazarevic. Were you ever aware of that practice where a document was entitled Joint Command and then it was signed by some VJ commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document. I think that Mr. Coo showed it to me in 2004 as well. I know of this one case when General Lazarevic signed a decision after the order of the Joint Command. I haven't come across any other instances, but I have an explanation for that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this order, the first order without an annex was a basis for coordination with the staff of the Ministry of the Interior, and in principle this was done in 1998 and in 1999 as a basis for coordination without any signature because as I've already said, the MUP did not accept the joint decisions in a different way without a signature. I studied this document very well, and this is what happened: In the first order, the basic idea of the commander was left out as the key basis for coordination because the decision of the commander is the basis for coordination. The plan is just form. This part is form. If you look at the first document, you do not have the commander's decision. Had I received this first document as a subordinate of General Lazarevic's, I wouldn't know what to do. So General Lazarevic probably noticed or one of his organs did that the basic idea was left out and then an additional paper was made along with the basic idea, and the basic idea has to be provided by the commander personally. Otherwise, it cannot constitute a basis for coordination either of the Ministry of the Interior or other structures. That is the only explanation, and I think that this is the right explanation because there are no other such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go back to P1966 for a minute, and if you can show me what you're talking about in terms of there's no decision made as to how or which forces are to be engaged? Do we need to look at what, paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four, that's the idea part of the decision. Without item 4, no order is valid. This is a rule in the army, and this basic idea is something that is adopted by the commander. There's always an item 4. No order, no matter what you're supposed to do, would not be valid without that because you have what he has decided the objective of the action, the combat disposition and readiness to execute the assignment, meaning movements of the units, and this was not issued by any one from the Joint Commander. It was issued by the commander of the Pristina Corps, the army commander, or the MUP Staff Commander, no one else. The person that had the command role issued it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, on the screen now on the right side, on the right-hand side, we have paragraph 4 from the original document I showed you, the Joint Command one with the unsigned "Joint Command" at the end. There is an item 4, and it appears to be nearly identical to the one that's in General Lazarevic's amendment, correct? I think the only difference I can see, and I'm just looking at the B/C/S, is that in General Lazarevic's amendment --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference. There is a difference. There are differences. That's where the problem lies. Look, there are differences. Because even if the sector is changed, the decision has to be changed as well. If the names of the sectors where the units are to go into action are changed, the decision has to be changed entirely. You cannot place just one sentence saying only that part of the decision is changed. You need to replace the whole decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see right from the beginning that there are changes. First you have Krpimej, Bradas, and in the other document you have Palahtna. This is the access, and that's the sector. There's major difference there. When we're talking about the axis, then it's indicated with three points, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. General Lazarevic testified about these two documents here in this trial, and he indicated that in his amendment the only thing he put in were the things that were different, and everything else from the original order remained in effect. Isn't that typically how an amendment would work? Rather than repeating the whole document, you only need to list the things that are changed.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see major changes here in comparison to the other items of the order. Only from what I can see, the decision is valid if there are corrections. If there are changes, it has to be redone. The measures are not so important for the subordinate units. They know which measures they're supposed to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something that General Stefanovic told us when he testified here, and it was at transcript pages 21661 through 662. Here's what he said. He said: "During the hand-over of my duty at the corps command, I was then told by General Djakovic... that the combat document entitled 'zapoveset' order is formulated for actions that are carried out by the army and the MUP, and the heading says 'Joint Command.' And instead of the commander's signature, where the signature should be, it says 'Joint Command,' as well, and also, there is this clause that all forces would be commanded by the Joint Command. "There are two forms there, two forms of these documents, one where in the heading and the signature it is the command of the Pristina Corps, rather, the commander with this clause of commanding the forces; that was more seldom, and then this other one that was more frequently present. In the heading it would say 'Joint Command,' and at the place where the signature of the commander is supposed to be, it also says 'Joint Command.' And when it says command, all forces will be commanded by the Joint Command. This was taken over from 1998, and it was only for situations where forces of the army and forces of the MUP were engaged," and the former order was in the computer. So if there are actions where there's joint activity by the MUP and VJ, this form was used with the Joint Command in the heading and in the signature block exclusively?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that the practice in 1998 as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if it was something that did not involve a joint action or support of the MUP by the VJ, then it would just be a Pristina Corps order, Pristina Corps command in the heading and a signature block signed by Pavkovic, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...help. If we could look at Exhibit P1428. And this relates to an action in the area of a couple of villages called Slup and Voksa, and I will tell you, in Exhibit P1468 there are some references to this action in these villages, but you see this is dated the 14th of August. It's decision on breaking up terrorist forces in the Slup and Voksa villages sector. The heading is "Pristina Corps command." Have you seen this one before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can remember, I worked on that document personally. I'm quite positive about that. And I do have some information if you wish to find out more about the document. The information is quite important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of specific questions first, and then I'll give you the opportunity to tell me that additional information. If we can go to the last page in both the B/C/S and the English. You will see that there is a signature block signed by -- and it's signed by General Lazarevic. And I will tell you from the Joint Command meetings notes that you took, there is a reference around this date. I don't have the precise page number with me right now, but where General Pavkovic advises the people attending that this action is going to be commanded by his -- his deputy, General Lazarevic. Now, if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I remember these records exactly. Not that General Lazarevic would command, but that he should command. So we need to put these questions very precisely. I would like to ask my colleague Mr. Hannis to be very precise when putting questions of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to the extent that that's what it says in P1468, I stand corrected, but we see his signature on this decision. And if we could go to the next to the last page in English. Keep the B/C/S where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see, General, in item number 6, it says -- there's a reference to the Joint Command there. It says: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." Now, I'm confused. Do you know why that reference is in this Pristina Corps command order signed by General Pavkovic? I --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Lazarevic, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two instructions or two books for the works -- work of commands and staffs. These are instructions or rules and attachment to the rules, and these are two basic documents based on which all combat and other documents are drafter from the general staff to the battalion. It is unified and defined specifically by levels who would be doing what. At one point after command and liaison or in one of sentences, you would put the sentence how to organise cooperation, coordination and joint action. I think in these instructions, this is defined with one to two sentences that -- so that these questions are defined in the order. Here, it's an unfortunate matter that the term is "Joint Command." I said that the Joint Command would be the MUP staff and the army command. I don't see Mr. Sainovic, Minic anywhere here because they were not at the Djakovica forward command post. I know that General Lazarevic was there. General Pavkovic was at the command post in Pristina, and General Lukic was at his command post at the MUP staff. This was definitely so because I attended conversations between General Lukic and General Pavkovic that they had occasionally. They would speak once or twice, sometimes even more often. I did attend some of these conversations between the two of them when these actions were being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe you need to help me with something in the translation, then, because my English says: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija with the Pristina Corps forward command post in Djakovica." Is that what it says in the B/C/S, with?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ask the witness to read that, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you read that first sentence under item number 6, "Command and communications."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for KiM, Kosovo and Metohija, with [as interpreted] the Pristina Corps forward command post in Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I noticed that in the original it appears --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, in the transcript there is a mistake. The witness correctly read it, but it was translated "with the Pristina Corps forward command post." It should not be "with," but it should be "from."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been translated in the document as "from." The whole point of it was to clarify it, and this interpreter also says "from." So can the interpreter assist us further?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is "from." "Sa" in this case is "from."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I put that the wrong way around. "With" would be used twice, but it's now been clarified as "from," Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I notice that the term for "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" in the original B/C/S is in bold print. Do you know why that would be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not any special practice. I don't know why. Probably in the typing at the automatic database-processing, the people who technically processed that perhaps wanted to emphasise that in particular in order to see that the decision to carry out combat actions was approved from both sides, from the MUP and from the command, but it's not anything special.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go up to item number 2. I think it's on the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we need to go back one more page on each to get to the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see the "Task for Units" involves VJ units supporting -- in some cases supporting a MUP unit, for example, in item 2.1. So part of this is a joint VJ/MUP action, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why, then, from what you explained me before does this document not have the header "Joint Command" and the signature block "Joint Command"? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that when this action was executed, I think that that day -- well, if you allow me to explain, to say what I wish to say. General Pavkovic asked General Samardzic to go to Djakovica, and the general asked him about this part, to break up the enemy in the area of Slup and Voksa, and he explained that the plan was drafted and that it will be brought up for approval, and General Samardzic asked him, who can explain that, and he said, Djakovic can. And he said, all right, let him bring it, and that evening, well, the general left, and he wasn't sure if he was going to come back. So pursuant to an approval by General Samardzic, I went to Djakovica. I don't know exactly why, perhaps because of these preparations. I personally took the decision to General Samardzic on the map for approval. He wanted me to explain about Slup, Voksa, and another preparatory action near Pec. So I spent an hour and a half explaining to him each element from the first paragraph to the last. He was satisfied, and then after that I called General Pavkovic because he couldn't come back that evening. I told him that the decision was approved. I assume that this is probably, then, the reason why the general signed it. The army general approved that the decision for support of the forces was approved, so I know there is a decision or, rather, a map in existence. I saw it, and I think Philip Coo in 2004 showed me that to see if that was actually General Samardzic's signature. I was present when he signed it. He said to me, Djakovic, give me that so I can sign it for you. That was his last sentence because that was the first time that I personally explained to General Samardzic the decision, him in the capacity of army General, and this I had to do because General Pavkovic was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to stop you there and move on because I have limited time. I'd like to show you Exhibit 6D716, which I think you were shown yesterday. This is a document dated the 19th of February, 1999. Do you remember this one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you wrote this one. Where were you at and what job did you have on the 19th of February 1999 that you would still be engaged in this activity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After handing over duties in late January, I remained in Pristina because General Mladenovic could not fit in. A lot of senior officers were being moved around, so all of these hand-over procedures had to be scheduled. So the official hand-over of duty between myself and General Mladenovic took place on the 20th or the 22nd of February. It began then, and it lasted until the 15th or the 16th of March. So from the 20th of January until the 20th of February, I was at the Pristina Corps command post and the forward command post of the 3rd Army in Gracanica. Occasionally, I went to the command post. I would assist in the drafting of documents. I took part in the drafting of plans relating to Thunder 3, Grom 3, which had to do with the duties of the army command in relation to the Pristina Corps command, and I was also preparing for the new duties that I was going to assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to compare this to an Exhibit P2808. Can we have a look at that on the screen for a moment. This is a document dated the 16th of February, 1999, from General Lazarevic. Have you seen this one before, General?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you see this one has the number 455-1, and that 455 series is -- is the number which all those Joint Command orders in March and April we see start with, that number 455. And -- and I will tell you that the 6D716 that you wrote appears to follow to a great extent what's set forth in this document, but you say you never saw it before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, the format of the document. That was not a combat document. It's, as we say, the template for an order that we had in our computer. All the information I could type in at any point in time, I could have it from the data-processing sector. I could have the template for that. But when you're executing combat actions, you need to put in axis and sectors, objectives. That was just a template that could even be in a textbook. Another thing is when it's defined by signature, by orders, it can be identical, of course, because that's how it was in the computer. I didn't need too much time to do that. I needed just enough time for the computer to process it and to bring it up as a general order that applied to all commands at specific levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you now about something in your unsigned statement taken by Mr. Coo in 2004 regarding Mr. Sainovic at paragraph 39. You were recorded as saying: "Mr. Sainovic was Deputy Federal Prime Minister, and as a part of his job he was in charge of some points of defence. I don't know exactly which, but this is a part of his job." Now, do you recall saying that in 2004 to Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, I need to say something. Leafing through yesterday, I found quickly somewhere, as much as I was able to leaf through the material, 21 incorrect assertions which I cannot stand behind. This was just at first glance, 21 incorrect assertions. I need to say something else. When I was speaking to Mr. Coo, I openly told him -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you just answer my question? I understand you may have found some -- and I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you, Your Honours. It's very important to let the witness to explain the circumstances in which he did not sign the statement to Philip Coo. Had the statement been signed, I would not be on my feet now, but he had refused to sign the statement. In order to evaluate the testimony, we need to hear what the witness has to say. Let's hear what the witness has to say about these 21 incorrect assertions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, this is not a statement that's before us as an exhibit in its entirety. There's no need for this to be explored. If you want to do it, Mr. Fila, you can do so. Mr. Hannis had a specific question, and the witness can answer that question. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First, General, could you just answer my question. Do you recall saying that to Mr. Coo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in this form.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in what form, then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Sainovic was deputy prime minister of the federal government, that from what I know he mainly carried out duties relating to the foreign political factor and duties arising from those conversations relating to internal questions of defence and relations with the Albanian people. That was related. That's what I said, which mainly had to do with conversations with Mr. Hill, Miles in Macedonia, in Belgrade, because I heard several times when Mr. Sainovic was saying how he was going for talks in Macedonia. Also, these conversations had to do with arming of the Siptar police forces in ethnically homogenous villages. This is something that I was talking to Mr. Coo about, not that he was responsible for questions of defence. The Defence questions, Mr. Minic spoke about from the aspect of functioning municipalities and regions together with Mr. Andjelkovic who dealt with the problems of civilian defence and civilian protection. This is what I spoke to him about. Now, perhaps he made a mistake or the interpreter made a mistake, I'm not sure which, but there are many such incorrect matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that you may have said that and don't remember, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. I asked the gentleman to allow me to look at the statement and that I sign it then, and he said no need. That's what he said the next day, and that's the way it remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- are you saying that Mr. Coo said there was no need for you to look at the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what he said, there was no need for me to sign it. I mean, I know, because everybody who made a statement from down there signed the statement except for me. I seem to be the only one. But you're not allowing me to say something which I believe is very important for the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You will probably get a chance from Mr. Fila later on, but isn't it correct that Mr. Coo tried to make arrangements with you to have this statement in English read back to you so you could make any changes or corrections as needed, but you declined to participate in that process? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. No, no, no. No. That is certainly not true. That is certainly not true. Twice I cautioned Mr. Coo. I'm telling you exactly the way it was. I'm not a man who says something that is not true. I cautioned Mr. Coo twice to the effect that the young lady was not writing things down when I was speaking. He was dictating the content of my statement, and I said since you're dictating, I cannot sign the statement without having looked at it. I said that quite openly because I'm not a person who signs something one day and on the next day says that that is not true. There are quite a few, many, correct things that Mr. Coo recorded. I'm not saying he changed everything. I'm not saying that. There are many things that are fair and correct that he wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I just want to be clear on this. Are you saying Mr. Coo did not provide you an opportunity or offer you the opportunity to hear what he had written in this statement before asking you to sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Bring him here. Let him face me. I am sure that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you, according to -- according to the statement, the interviews occurred on three different dates, 26th and 27th of March, 2004, and the 22nd of October, 2004. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that, but on the 22nd of October that was an interview that took an hour, an hour and a half, and it only had to do with some of my functional duties because I wasn't sure when it was that I took over duty when I handed over to someone else. Quite simply, I hadn't been prepared for that interview, and I wasn't aware of the content of the interview. He asked me very specifically about the times involved, the times of hand-over, and I simply wasn't sure after several years when it happened. So even now I had to go to the personnel department to look at documentation and see when it was that I handed over duty and when it was that I took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move to another topic, then, and ask you about Exhibit P2068. You were shown this document yesterday. This is a document that's entitled "Instructions for the Defence --" well, that doesn't appear to be the right document. I'm sorry. I may have transposed my digits. I need 2086. I may have said 68. My apologies. 2086 is a document that's entitled "Instructions for the defence of populated areas. Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," and it's dated July 1998. You told us yesterday in describing this that -- you said at page 55, line 17: "This looks to me like a training exercise for how to do the defence of inhabited areas," and you went on to say this isn't binding on anyone, it doesn't oblige anyone, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you a related Exhibit, P1064. This is dated the 28th of July, 1998. It's from Petar Ilic, the chief of defence administration in the administrative defence, and you'll see it makes reference to these instructions for the defence of residential areas. It says they're attached to this cover letter, and you will see the first paragraph says: "The joint demand for Kosovo and Metohija has issued instructions for the defence of inhabited areas ..." And in paragraph 2, he makes reference to the resubordination of conscripts from the Federal Ministry of Defence units formed and mobilised by the defence departments and sections to the MUP. And in the third paragraph, he says: "We would point out that the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija has determined a new composition of municipal defence staffs, and in addition to representatives of local self-governed units, the MUP, the Municipal Assembly, Executive Committee, and the VJ, chiefs of defence departments and heads of defence sections have also become members of these staffs." Now, from your position and in your participation in taking notes for the meetings of the Joint Command from the 22nd of July, 1998, you weren't aware that this was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically as far as this document is concerned, I didn't know about it, but I did have contacts with Mr. Ilic otherwise, who was on the fourth or the fifth floor of our command. That is to say that is where his headquarters were. I had contacts with him up to January, February 1999. Yesterday, I said in relation to these instructions that I assume that most probably the administration in the defence ministry had this instruction by way of a general instruction for the defence of inhabited areas, so I assume that Mr. Ilic, knowing in our conversations that we had meetings with representatives of the MUP and the political representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that he also wrote this up in this text with the intention of raising --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're going well beyond my question now, I think, and I need to try and move on. Isn't it a fact that this issue of defence plans for the towns, for populated areas, was a topic that was discussed in those Joint Command meetings that you were taking notes of in late July 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was stated, yes, but plans were not made. So no plans were made at meetings. Mr. Minic only stated that there was information from municipalities and districts. That is certainly the way it was, sir, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you if plans were made at the meetings. Would you look at P1468. Do you have your hard copy with you, the minutes or the meeting notes for the Joint Command? I'm looking at page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S, the first meeting on the 22nd of July, 1988. There are five items listed at the beginning, which I take it are the agenda items. Number 2 is: "Measures for the defence of the towns and measures for Pec." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you will go over to page 3 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's page 469 English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see Mr. Minic speaking, and then there's item number 2: "There's a danger of attacks on the towns." General -- "No town can fall into Siptar hands. General Pavkovic is to give instructions. Priority is to be given to the crisis towns ..." Then that next sentence, can you help me? I have an illegible word here in English that I don't understand. It says: "We have to have measures, forces and control." Can you read that sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not really following this yet. Where is it that you're reading from? Is it page 2 or page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's page 3. You see item number 2? Page 1 may be the -- it's on the screen. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my page 2. "There is a danger of towns being attacked." It is page 2 in my version, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the list of towns there, can you read us the rest of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We have to have an assessment, measures, forces, and control. The staff consists of the president of the municipality, the government, the army, the MUP, and the National Defence Department. At the level of the district, the chief, the MUP, and the army will meet."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And could you go on to page 4 or the next page for you. I think I have to subtract one because I'm using the electronic version, which includes the cover page as page number 1. But the next page for you, you see Mr. Gajo speaks, and below his remarks there's a conclusion, and it says, does it not, that "Pec and Suva Reka have defence plans, but other towns need to be worked on; Djakovica of special interest." Right? Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have it on page 3. Oh, the conclusion. Yes, yes. I do apologise. Yes, the conclusion. You're asking me about that, to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Did I read it correctly, that Pec and Suva Reka have defence plans, but other towns need --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it seems yesterday you were trying to suggest that these Joint Command instructions for defence of towns were something that were maybe just a staff exercise for somebody. These were instructions that came from the Joint Command. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not from the Joint Command. That document, the instructions were in the corps command, and every structure has instructions like that by way of a reminder for their work on defending inhabited areas and towns. So there is the ministry that has that and the army that has that. I don't know about the MUP. I never saw that, but as for the structure of the ministry, I'm sure about the federal ministry because I had exceptionally good cooperation were Mr. Ilic, and I had regular contacts with him. I know that for sure because I stayed in Kosovo before that, as well, from '88 until '92, and I know -- I've known since then that these instructions exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Djakovic, you've answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on that contact and good cooperation with Mr. Ilic, why would he be putting -- or referring to these instructions as being instructions from the Joint Command if, as you say, they came from the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the same reasons that we had for using this, so the members from the other structures -- well, since no one was subordinated to anyone, this was done in order for us to coordinate certain activities. The question is that without this, Ilic would carry out these obligations of coordination because he is not the mainstay of coordination of the territory, but quite simply now, in a way he is referring to that so that people could take this more seriously, their obligations in terms of defending inhabited areas and towns because he had part of his units dealing with that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't think that makes any sense. Why would he need something like that to make the people he was sending these instructions to take it more seriously? Didn't he have authority over those members of the civil defence and civil protection that were part of the Ministry of Defence? He had authority. He didn't need to invoke the words "Joint Command" to make anybody take anything more seriously, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, but only over his own part of the structure, as it were, along the vertical line. He had two lines below him. Two levels below him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that as far as you know, the Joint Command as -- and I'm using the term as describing the people who met at the meetings in your notebook. You're saying as far as you know, there were not meetings of the Joint Command in 1999, is that right, in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will tell you that General Lukic gave an interview to the OTP, and he told us that the Joint Command met in 1999 at page 112 of his interview, which is Exhibit P948. And he was asked, "During the time of the bombing, where would the Joint Command be more often?" He said the meetings were held at whatever -- at whichever location we could. He said, "Now it's all coming back to me. Speaking of the places where the meetings were held, they were usually held in basements, but most often they were held in the shelter of the Grand Hotel." You didn't know about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1999, I no longer attended any of these meetings. I even did not attend meetings with the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say with their organs, because I was within the army. I said that I only had two or three contacts with members of the MUP through commissions, through the order on the resubordination of the MUP, a few contacts like that. However, I had no other direct contacts with the representatives of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we look at Exhibit P2016, please. General, this is a document from the 25th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I'm not objecting to what Mr. Hannis is asking now, but I waited for the answer to be completed. I'm asking you for instructions. If General Lukic's statement is being used, a statement given to an investigator, and it's been said that it cannot be used to the detriment of others, it seems to me that what Mr. Hannis did a few moments ago could have been detrimental. So now I would be interested in hearing what you as the Trial Chamber think in relation to this question and answer because it could have been detrimental. Now, I really don't know whether I should complain. If I shouldn't, then I do apologise, but I waited just in case so as not to harm Mr. Hannis in any way, especially if I'm not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, all we have is the witnesses's understanding of the situation. He's made it clear he doesn't know anything about what is in General Lukic's statement, and that is it. We can only take the evidence as the witness gives it, no more, no less. There's nothing more to be said. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is from the 25th of April, 1999. It's a combat report to the 3rd Army command and the Supreme Command Staff from the Pristina Corps command. If we could go to page 2 in both the English and B/C/S, I have a question I want to ask you about a comment here. It's -- I'm sorry. We have to go back to page 1 of the B/C/S, I guess. I need to find item 2.1. Thank you. You see item 2.1.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Operations of combing the terrain and breaking up the Siptar terrorists continue in line with the decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." That suggests to me that in April 1999, the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija apparently is still functioning and making decisions. You have no reason to disagree with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can agree in part but only in the context of that conversation and my explanation of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, are we nearing the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are we nearing the end? Is that your question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I know I'm over the time I told Your Honours. I probably need 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This session, I think, Mr. Hannis, focus on what's most important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you next Exhibit P1281, and if we could go down to the bottom of the page in English. This is from the VJ web site, and it deals with a public discussion that apparently was taking place between General Pavkovic and Dusan Mihajlovic, who was the minister of the interior at the time, related to alleged crimes in connection with the freezer truck with dead bodies in it. Were you familiar with that public event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to go to page number 2 of the English, and I'll read it to you, General. I'm not sure where it is on the B/C/S, but General Pavkovic is saying: "The police had their own headquarters headed by their own officers, and the cooperation with the army was coordinated through political actors in joint command formed for the purpose. Therefore, the information to what the police force units were doing can best be provided by the police commanders and members of the joint command in charge of them." Would you agree with General Pavkovic that the Joint Command was formed for the purpose of coordinating MUP and VJ activities? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know if this is his statement. I mean, I personally never heard that kind of statement from General Pavkovic. In what context was it given? I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Set that aside for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm assuming since it's on the VJ web site and it says he said that. Assume he said that. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us assume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you agree that the Joint Command was formed so that the cooperation between the VJ and the army could be coordinated through the political actors in the Joint Command? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the part that I'm talking about in terms of the Joint Command, the staff of the MUP, and the army, yes. That is to say as far as General Lukic is concerned and General Pavkovic as commanders of certain formations as a joint command that coordinated activities, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you don't agree with the part where General Pavkovic said that the cooperation between the police and the army was coordinated through political actors in the Joint Command. Is that your answer, you do not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part. Just in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what the radio call-sign was for the Pristina Corps command and the forward command post in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 1998? Well, these things changed whenever there was an action or a plan. I mean, it wasn't a constant thing, or at least that's not what I recall. I don't recall a call-sign that was a permanent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis, have you allowed Defence counsel to see that document with the highlighted passages?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told it's too big to e-mail. We are making -- we're trying to make colour copies with the highlighted sections. Mr. Reid told me it might be possible to make a CD.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps we can deal with this. Mr. Hannis would like the witness to try to deal with the illegible passages, and I gather there's about 80 of them that he's identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah 84, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is there any objection to this? Does anyone feel strongly against it? No. Well, it would be unwise, I think, to use everybody's time. Obviously, anyone who wants to be there when it's done can be there, but there seems little point, and one way of doing it would be to use Rule 71 of the Rules, which would be a deposition process that Mr. Haider could supervise, and the OTP could simply ask the witness to read the various passages, and the interpreter would translate them, and that would be recorded and then a compilation document could be framed thereafter. Now, maybe it could be done more informally that. In other words, we could follow Rule 71 but not necessarily comply with all the requirements. What we'll do is consider the possibilities and try to set that up for tomorrow, and that would allow Mr. Djakovic to complete his evidence and this exercise tomorrow and get back home, which I'm sure he's anxious to do. If -- can you tell me at the moment whether it's likely the Defence cross-examination will take the rest of today? Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Lukic, can you help?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that we'll have some of my colleagues crossing this witness before me, but I think that we have pretty lengthy cross-examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We might going into tomorrow, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's likely that we might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But hopefully there would be time still tomorrow to conduct this other exercise, as well, and review it the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I certainly invite the Defence if there are any illegible portions that they're interested in that aren't on my list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we know that Mr. Fila has an interest in this having identified all the illegible portions in an earlier filing and no doubt assisted you by doing so, so he may wish to identify some. I'm not sure, but I think his principle concern is that we get as much accurate information as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need our break again at this stage, Mr. Djakovic, for 20 minutes. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will resume again at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're working on a way of dealing with these minutes in the course of tomorrow, and we'll inform you later in the day of the exact arrangements. Note -- sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, wouldn't it be the easiest thing for the translators to sit with Djakovic this afternoon, for them to do that this afternoon, and we would have that in the morning, either formally or informally? It seems to me that's the simplest thing in the world. This guy's reading, and the interpreter is translating, and that's it. Then we would all be happy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's okay with the witness, yes, it sounds a good idea. We'll deal with that, then, at the end of today's business. Before we move on, Judge Chowhan has a question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: If you go back to page 6, line 1, of your statement, you had said that the politicians were there, and you've given the names, for performance of certain functions. Would you be kind enough in elaborating what those functions were which required their presence there? That's very kind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what I noticed, and that is that at the meeting they showed interest for certain questions, and the way I saw them during that hour or hour and a half during those briefings, after the briefings I would really not see any more of them because they would have work to do in the field or in the offices of the Executive Council. I don't know where they would go later. The meetings were usually held in the evening and would take an hour to two hours. Exceptionally, sometimes we would have meetings also with the MUP in order to coordinate during the day or in the morning. What I can say about Mr. Minic is this: I noticed that he mainly dealt with tasks relating to the functioning of the municipal organs, organs of the district, and he had a lot in common with Mr. Andjelkovic as far as resolving civilian protection issues. Mr. Sainovic mostly reported back about questions that had to do with the foreign policy factor. I said that he often had talks with Mr. Hill, Miles, and some other representatives, and from what I can remember, I think that he was away some 13 times from these meetings during these 60 or 64 days that I was taking the minutes. This was the number of times that he was absent. He would often go to Belgrade, to Macedonia. He had meetings in Kosovo. I heard a couple of times when he commented. I was following that from the sidelines, when he spoke with Mr. Minic and said that he had preparations for talks with Mr. Hill. In two days he was going to Macedonia. He needed to prepare well to talk about the platform for the talks. This is what I heard. I know that after talks with Mr. Hill, he intensively supported the implementation of decisions that he had said that Mr. Hill agreed to, and this had to do with the forming of ethnic police in ethnic villages. Actually, Albanian policemen in ethnically Albanian villages, for them to carry out security in the village themselves, to be equipped with uniforms, with insignia, with sidearms meaning pistols, and he did say that at least they should resemble a police force so that the people would accept them. This is what he did. Occasionally, he would comment if any of the commanders would report on some questions that had to do with military activities in terms that the army did such-and-such a thing. In the course of the day, he would put some questions that had to do with what the plan was for the following day, if the commander approved a decision, meaning General Samardzic, and things like that. So these questions were put sometimes. Andjelkovic mostly dealt with civilian protection and civilian defence matters, and as far as I know from what I could see of those people, he's the only person that I saw three or four times in 1999, once in Kosovska Mitrovica and maybe twice in Pristina. I saw him in passing. And as for Matkovic, I saw him a couple of times he came. I didn't see him that often. I saw him mostly because he was also an MP, a representative of the Socialist Party in the parliament, and as far as I know he had some companies in Kosovo because he was also the director of Sartid, and so mostly things that had to do with these economic issues, and whenever economic issues were up in these briefings, then he would emphasise these questions. This is what I saw of him. In the notebooks, I actually made an analysis of all of these discussions in a way because I was purely interested to see what I noted down during those 64 or 65 days when I was practically taking these minutes, these notes. This is how I saw those people. General Samardzic was present at the meetings. He would attend. The army commander. There are at least -- there was one discussion of his from the 27th. I remember that, and that was the basis, let me put it that way. And nobody ever questioned the army commander's decisions, never. I've already mentioned one instance when simply relating to that question, the question of issues and orders, nobody asked questions. If there was some request, it would be the general's request, either a request by General Lukic or some proposal from the other members: Would this be good, would this be possible, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: General, thank you very much for that elaborate answer, but it looks a bit strange to have a composition like that. There must be somebody who must be convening these meetings. Now, whose idea it was to induct the politicians also there, and what was the rationale behind that idea? Because as a matter of fact, if it was merely a question of briefing simpliciter, well, we know what briefing is. It could be done man to man, so this -- and then in these meetings what you were discussing with some plans, also, and so on, could you just throw some light on this, please, with all your background and expertise and your presence there? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot say exactly whose idea it was, but based on what I know I believe the idea probably came from Belgrade for them to come down to Kosovo. As for the specific assignments that they were given, that I don't know. This is something that I cannot really comment on. I'm just giving my impressions from these meetings, from these talks, briefings, and so on and so forth. How it was scheduled, well, let's say the first meeting. I said how I came to attend the first meeting. Mr. Minic was the president or the chairman of the council of citizens, and realistically speaking, he had the highest post out of all the civilians. Then he was followed by Mr. Sainovic. I'm talking about my assessment. Followed by Mr. Andjelkovic, and then either Gospodin Matkovic or Mr. Andjelkovic. Probably more likely, it was Mr. Andjelkovic. I'm not sure, but it seemed to me that Mr. Minic, when he was at the meeting, in a way was the one who -- let's say, was the one who put the most questions, spoke whether we needed to see each other again or not, whether it was necessary for them to come and report back about something again or not. When he was there, he was the first one to actually state the agenda, and if army briefings are in question, there is no agenda. The briefing proceeds along the elements of combat readiness, and this is done by commanders -- and this is done pursuant to six elements of combat readiness. We never discussed -- or the briefings did not go in the order of the combat readiness items. We were talking about political relations, Albanians, Serbs, the Serbian state, political leadership of Kosovo. We discussed political matters of broader significance, not just of Serbian significance but the Balkans and the European question. There was no briefing based on the elements because if this was the case, the commander who was in charge would then issue assignments and the deadlines when these assignments had to be implemented, but this was not there. Had these tasks been issued, I would surely have written that down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: With a person as senior as a deputy prime minister present there, well, can it be said that he was also imparting instructions, or was he just sitting and listening without showing any leadership there? What have you to say on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't sitting there without being interested in what was going on. As for the reasons why he was interested, I'm thinking now. If he was carrying out the post of dealing with this foreign policy moment, then of course it was -- he was interested to know what the situation in the field was, and the only opportunity was to get the information from General Lukic and from General Pavkovic, from the army commander, from General Djordjevic, from Obrad and from the others who participated in all of that. And also from Mr. Minic for them to mutually exchange information through the municipal organs, the district organs, through the civilian structures, from the ministry, and so on and so forth. The only opportunity was for him there to get good information so that he had a good basis to speak with someone because if we're going for talks with someone, you have to prepare. You have to think about what the situation is. You cannot just go. At least this is how I viewed it. You cannot go for talks with someone without knowing what the situation is in the territory and then make assertions. A witness who comes to testify has to look at something. He has to see documents because he cannot remember everything. And I -- I am sure that and I'm saying that only at those meetings and briefings they lasted for an hour and a half, and then for the rest of their work hours and for the whole rest of the afternoon, they were carrying out duties that I don't know what they were. Probably in the Executive Council. I know that Mr. Matkovic would come and talk -- or to resolve problems that had to do with the electrical supply installations, to resolve problems about that. There was another gentleman who would come, Andre, Andre Milosavljevic I think his name was. He was also from the government. He was there to resolve the problems of repairing houses, issue humanitarian aid in Malisevo, to the refugees in Malisevo, in areas where there was demolition. They would glass in the windows, and this is all from the notes that are practically, practically recording that, and all these things were interesting to me, and I wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Since they were coming, perhaps, as you said, on instructions from Belgrade, well, a person of that level coming there and being present in those meetings, did he express that he was carrying some instructions? Did he guide you in any respect? Did he differ with you in any respect stating that this was the Belgrade's policy or in view of that policy, or just he would be just sitting most of the time getting briefings and listening to you? I mean, coming all the way from Belgrade, he must be carrying some instructions and guiding you on those instructions. Did he perform such -- did he act in that way or what? Can you kindly elucidate. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will try to elucidate. I know that usually at these meetings, no contacts with Belgrade and that part were mentioned, rather, whether he or any of them spoke with anybody from Belgrade. That is something I don't know. That is not present to me as for -- if the deputy prime minister spoke with the prime minister or any other members, I don't know. I wasn't present. What I do know is that in these notes, there isn't half as much written down as was actually said on these political topics. I said that I wrote down the least about that part concerning talks with Mr. Hill. That was pure politics, and I as a soldier wasn't really interested in that. I was entrusted with a specific function, and I never received any kind of indication or suggestion to try to resolve something that somebody else would provide a basis for. I was only ordered by General Pavkovic or the army commander. I was away from General Lazarevic, even though he was my first-ranking superior. I was away from him. He was in Djakovica, and I was in Pristina, so practically I would only occasionally communicate with General Lazarevic, and I cannot simply know whether they had communications with others outside of that group amongst themselves. That is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, no questions, have you? All right. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to carry on with this line. Yesterday, to a question by Judge Bonomy, and this is page 26380, you said, and I'm paraphrasing, that at the point in time when these meetings were held, which were also attended by civilians, you already had an order from General Samardzic. So I am going to tell you that General Simic also testified here, who was at the 3rd Army forward command post in Pristina at the time, and that he said that General Pavkovic would come to him with an order that he needed to approve for the following day, and then after that you would go to the meeting -- the meetings only after this order was approved, that some orders were given by Samardzic and some by Simic. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you would then go to the meeting with such an order. Well, now let us bring to a logical conclusion this line of questioning started by Judge Chowhan. So whatever any of those four civilians said, could that have any influence on an order that was already made or to the chain of command of the army of Yugoslavia in any event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could only in one case, and that would be to submit a request to General Pavkovic for him to report to the army commander and for the army commander to correct or augment his decision. There would be no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So this request would go from where, from civilians or from whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
