utterances.text: Well, mainly from the MUP. The MUP usually would submit things for the helicopter and for this, for that. The requests would initiate -- be initiated by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the gap. There's already a problem building up. Just slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then the technology was that Pavkovic would again need to go to Samardzic for approval.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then when Samardzic -- or, rather, Simic, because we're treating them the same, approved that, that would be that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the decision never went there to the meeting. The general would only note that the decision was approved. The document itself never went to that part. I would never take the map to that meeting and say, "General Samardzic has approved it, here." No. It was enough for them to say -- for General Pavkovic to say that the decision was approved, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Would you agree with me, then, that any suggestion or anything that the four said did not have any influence on what was done?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Their influence was not really that significant, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The second question that I have arising from a question from Mr. Hannis, and we're talking about this operative inter-resource staff document that you were reading from where Mr. Hannis asked you to read where the Joint Command is being met --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At one point, the Prosecutor stopped you. You said you were familiar with the contents. Did you ever prepare anything for General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would prepare for the Pristina Corps information with which General Pavkovic, General Samardzic, and General Perisic, and General Dimitrijevic, until the end of 1998 while practically the meetings were going on up there would go to brief about the situation in the Pristina Corps and the territory. This is what the briefings would be about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. And these would be briefings on military matters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What I'm interested is -- is was there any mention of civilians or anything who were saying something there or commanding in these preparations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No mention of anything like that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this unsigned statement of yours that you gave to Philip Coo, did you ever have a translation of your statement into Serbian so you could read it, look at it, agree to it, and then sign it? Was this opportunity ever given to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how did he introduce himself? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first time I heard who Philip Coo was, I heard about that here. I had information from my colleagues a year or two ago who testified, who said that he was an expert. Some expert; I don't know what he was doing. But I don't have information about it. I cannot really state if it was even him. I simply didn't notice. I didn't write it down. I didn't write down who this person is that I was talking to, but I can see by the team who was there, I think that there was lady with him also who was doing the work, but I didn't know of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that you never saw that statement? It was never presented to you to read and to sign?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up in e-court 4D525. Could it please be zoomed in a bit. Do you recognise the document, General? I have it in hard copy, too, if that will be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have seen the document because it's an army document, an army command document, but when I was in the Pristina Corps, as for the content --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Please look at the bottom of the document. Who was it sent to? If we can have it scrolled down a bit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And as I've said, this document was probably addressed straight away to the commander of the Pristina Corps. That is to say that I did not receive all the documents that were coming in from the army. I mean, they went through the office, and they would go to the main persons involved. And part of the documents that have to do with the operations organ the commander would address to me. And part of the documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That will do, General. That will do. Do you know since you were there in Pristina in the summer of 1998 that every day, briefings were held at the forward command post of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who chaired these briefings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the briefings there was the commander of the army, the chief of staff. I am trying to remember now. Then the chief of the operations department. Then there was one of the assistants from logistics. Then there was the head of intelligence on a regular basis. So it was the organs of the command of the army. Between 10 and 15 persons, depending on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And from time to time you were present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was discussed there -- or, rather, what the briefings were about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was daily activities that were discussed. It had to do with the elements of combat readiness, as we put it, and problems were discussed, and usually we would take our decisions for approval by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me interrupt you at this point. Can we now call up 4D529.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to give the document to the witness in hard copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. In B/C/S it is page 2, the one but last paragraph, and in English it is page 5. And there is an abbreviation there in the document that says -- it seems that you're the person speaking there towards the end of the document. It says "The chief."

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you please read that part?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the first or second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The second page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Combat group 15-2 to the north of the village of Rakovina today around noon repelled the attack of the DTS from the area of the village of Crnljane and the village of Gaj on which occasion 20 terrorists were killed. During the day, preparations were being carried out for the Ratis operation -- or action. The brigade commands and the combat groups were doing the planning. The action starts the day after tomorrow, on the 8th of September." And on the last page, the one but last paragraph and the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the department, that is to say I, explaining the decision of the commander concerning Ratis and also in Papracane. "There is a barracks with about 1.000 to 1.200 terrorists. The objective is to carry out an action very swiftly in order to find mass graves. Later, the command of the PRK is to plan action to Baranski Lug because otherwise part of the forces will ensure things from this direction."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We did not hear the question or answer because the previous answer didn't finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will finish. I will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, could you repeat this. After you were speaking, after you explained, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just repeat the answer for it to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the army personally approved it like -- for Ratis like he did in the previous cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to that, can we call up in e-court 6D1643. Could it be please be zoomed in. Not that much. Not that much, please. General, in the lower right-hand corner, can you see the signature?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the signature of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could we see the upper part of the map now. Am I right? Is this the decision map for the action that we spoke of just now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, that's it. On the left, there is the approval of the commander, and on the right-hand side is the signature of the commander of the unit whose forces are carrying out the action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can we have a look at 4D528 now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would kindly ask the usher to give the witness this document in hard copy as well. Could we please have 4D528 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, can you please have a look at the B/C/S version. In Serbian it's page 2, item 4, under (a) and (b), and in English it is on page 4. Just tell us first and foremost, General, from whom did this document come; who is it addressed to; and finally, what does item 4 say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the command of the 3rd Army. It was signed by the army commander after the team from the General Staff toured, I think it was between the 13th and the 15th of August, and on the basis of that he issued specific orders with regard to all elements of combat readiness and in relation to all tasks to the Pristina Corps, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us now what the specific tasks are in item 4 under (a) and (b)?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, number 4 is a task in cooperation and coordination with the MUP forces and in accordance with the deployment of forces in the area to prevent the spill-over of forces from the KiM area into the Rasko-polimlje district and also in the Jablanica and Pcinja district. The mainstay of this activity are the army command and the commander of the Pristina Corps. And the deadline says continuous task.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (b), continue coordination and coordinated action with the MUP forces and in accordance with the assessments, provide support to the MUP forces in breaking up sabotage and terrorist groups using measures that will not significantly affect the completion of the primary tasks, the securing of the state border, and the defence of all military facilities, units, and commands. "The mainstay of this activity is the army command and the Pristina Corps command. The deadline, continuous task."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said in the introduction of this document, the commander invokes General Perisic's document 4D416. I said that only for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we please call up in e-court now 4D531. General, this is a brief document. Could you just take a look at it and tell me what this is about? Or, rather, who the author is, to who it was sent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand when I read the last sentence, I realised what this was all about. This is an order by which the army commander forms new combat groups in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and in line with his own authority. Before that, what had been established were forces on the basis of a special order in terms of standing combat readiness levels of the chief of staff throughout the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and this was done in a unified manner. So now the army commander as the authorised officer is forming new combat groups as temporary units for carrying out specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: At the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the proposal of the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, yesterday, on page 46, lines 13 through 22 in the transcript of your testimony here today -- here yesterday, you said that General Pavkovic gave you some special tasks before the OSCE mission arrived, and you said something about the deployment of units in the area. So could we now please look at 4D381. It's a map, so you will have a look. Please take a look at this map and tell me, can you recognise it? What is on this map? I have a hard copy, too, in black and white if it will be easier for you to compare.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be easier. I mean, I know about this map. This is what I explained in a way until now. This is the deployment of forces because on the 16th of October, an agreement was signed with the mission. I -- the mission of the OSCE, that is, on the withdrawal of the army and police from the territory. What was regulated was that three combat groups should be left -- or, rather -- I beg your pardon. Three tactical -- well, yes, combat groups at company level, at company level in the area of Kremovic [phoen]. This is combat group 125/5. Then in the area of Iglarevo. That is combat group 15/3. And combat group in Dulje, 243/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So this map corresponds to the situation that you talked about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I worked on that in accordance with the order issued to me by General Pavkovic that we should prepare these forces, that we should withdraw the other forces into barracks and carry out our tasks, and that is why I interrupted the activities involved in until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: So this was approved by General Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All tasks. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, yesterday on page 28, lines 5 through 8, you said - I'm moving to 1999 now - that in 1999 you had only two contacts as far as the MUP was concerned. One was on the 19th of April after you received an order from the General Staff on resubordination, and the second one you talked about had to do with Istok. I'm interested in the contact you had on the 19th of April. Can you remember who was present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime in the afternoon, 4.00 or 5.00. It could have been around that time. Between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon on the 19th. The members of the police -- or, rather, General Djordjevic, General Obrad Stefanovic, and General Lukic came. Now, I'm not 100 per cent sure where this meeting took place. Well, they came at the invitation of General Pavkovic, I believe, and I didn't know what would be discussed. General Lazarevic was there and a few other officers from the command. And then General Pavkovic gave General Djordjevic a telegram from the General Staff that he read. He didn't read it out loud, but General Djordjevic did read it, and he returned it to General Pavkovic. I mean, he returned this telegram. And a certain explanation was provided. And I know that the question of resubordination was there in relation to the telegram sent by the chief of General Staff in terms of resubordinating the members of the MUP to the Pristina Corps. So that was the content of the telegram because afterwards I took the telegram with me. I had it in the archives then. Quite simply, I mean -- well, what the reaction was. Well, the reaction of General Djordjevic, well, I have to say exactly what happened. He said, what do you mean Ojdanic? Who is he going to command? Those were his words. We were all taken a bit by surprise, and practically they, the members of the MUP, still did not accept that the army would command practically in the entire zone or in the area of Kosovo. In a way, they remained on the basis of coordination as before, or someone -- or everyone carried out their own activities independently in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will move to another topic. Yesterday and today, General, you told us that you cooperated closely with General Pavkovic, and I believe that you're familiar with his numerous orders about respecting international humanitarian law, and you probably drafted most of them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you know any of his written or oral orders when he addressed his subordinate units or superiors where he asked the opposite from them of respect of international war on humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the things that I know about how General Pavkovic acted towards civilians, towards the wounded, towards prisoners of war have a lot of examples where I can show that these were actually implemented in practice. As of June, he tried by all available means to get in touch with the Albanian -- let's say some village -- key people who were conducting the village policy in a way, and his conversation is known down there, and I was present as well as the assistant for morale and a group of people when he received, received support from the Albanian people in the village of Brovina, the village of Morici, and places where he conducted talks with those people and the promise that he would not allow terrorists to enter the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We already have evidence about that. General, my last question is this. Yesterday and today, you talked in detail about this. You as an operative officer at the post where you were, are you aware that there was ever any kind of plan to expel the Albanian civilian population in order to change the balance of the population that would remain in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sure of that. In 1998, I had the plans. My man handled all the plans in 1998 in the Pristina Corps. There wasn't even a draft of such a plan, never mind that it was actually done. In order to make such a plan, a larger group of people would need to work on it. So practically there is no chance that any such plan ever existed. I never heard that there was such a plan with the MUP, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, 57, 22. I believe the witness said in the village of Brovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Freudian slip, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Brovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one clarification. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: General, you said in this context that the General Pavkovic had in June with these local representatives of the population. When was this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998, before the conflict. This is when the clashes on the border were just starting. There were only clashes on the border, but there were no major clashes on the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am going to be even more brief than my colleague Mr. Aleksic. I have some questions for you, and since you have already talked about and have mentioned the team from the General Staff, I would like to ask you -- and Mr. Hannis showed you Exhibit P1468 [as interpreted]. If you recall, this is an order by the Pristina Corps for Stup Ivoksa [phoen]. You had explained that you had been to seen General Samardzic to report to him. In relation to that action, I'm interested if you recall -- I apologise. I gave you the wrong number. It doesn't matter. You recall the order that was shown by my colleague Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you recall that at that time it was actually the team of the General staff which you said had been in Kosovo at the time when this action was executed, was actually at the forward command post in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at the time of certain activities down there at the border, General Perisic was there personally at Planeja, but I cannot really link it up. I'm not quite sure if I could say that that happened at that particular moment, but I can say that there were conflicts at Planeja, around Ponosevac, and this was a action that was executed for sure. I know that well. But it would be hard for me to connect that that happened at that particular time. It's been ten years since then, since that event. I would need to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, General, sir. We did hear the testimony of General Obradovic here.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when General Perisic was there, I know that there were conflicts and I -- that Commander Pavkovic was there at Planeja, that this is an elevation near Ponosevac, and that fighting was being conducted there, and he was there personally. He watched it happen, and he issued assignments in the sense of securing the state border, joint action and coordination with the MUP and so on and so forth, and the general later told me about this conversation later when they came back. I was personally not there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, thank you, and just for the transcript, a correction: The order is P1428. That is the order, not P1468. General, sir, can we now clarify just one more thing. You said that on the 20th of January you handed over your duties --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You handed over your duty, and you said that up until the 20th of February -- yesterday, you said that General Stefanovic in late December 1998 took over duties.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: However, I'm going to show you from his testimony, will you please agree --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Perhaps I said something wrong. We started our hand-over then, but the hand-over was completed around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Stefanovic testified here. I would now like to -- you to concentrate on my question. In December, late December 1998, a decision was made on his appointment to your post, and also, in December 1998 the decision was made for you to go to the army.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General Stefanovic said and also in a conversation he said that he remembers very well that it is his Slava, his saint's day on the 20th of January, and that that day he came to the corps to assume duty -- his duties, and this lasted until the 20th of February, and this corresponds to what you have just said, that on the 20th you handed over your duty and that this was completed on 20th of February. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if it was exactly like that, but it's possible that I am mistaken. I'm not able to -- well, I have the impression that I handed over my duties to him, and it went on for quite a long time, from late December. It was not only the hand-over. I was also introducing him into the functions. He hadn't assumed duties in December and January, meaning he was not able to. He hadn't signed that. There were special documents that need to be signed, so he was unable to do that. But the hand-over did last for a while, so perhaps we don't agree. This does not quite correspond in -- with some 10 or 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now you have clarified that. Can we now look at Exhibit 1166, please. P1166. It's a Prosecution document. This is an order which is entitled "Order." It's 1966. I apologise once more. It's an order for the break-up of Siptar terrorists in the sector of Malo Kosovo. Please, can you look at paragraph marked with the number 4. Let's look at that. Is readiness mentioned in this order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last page of this order now. Does it say to whom the order is addressed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at the next document, which is augmentation, an addition to this document. This is 1967. And can you please tell me in paragraph 4 in this supplement, is there any mention of readiness?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, readiness is defined here. That is why to a certain extent besides what I already explained to the Prosecutor the readiness is also defined here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2 now. Can we look at the last page. Can you please tell me, General Lazarevic's signature is in the left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which documents are signed in the left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones with the weight of an order. Oh, you mean in the left corner. It's like a telegram. That sort of document would be sent -- would be signed to the left. The documents that have the force of an order are signed to the left and the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Does the telegram have to be signed when it is sent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A telegram can be sent. It doesn't have to be signed, but the person who sends it off can send it off and forward it pursuant to authorisation. You have such information. For example, the duty operations officer in the combat operations centre would send out combat reports pursuant to authorisation by the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You really need to observe the pause, but there is a point that seems to need clarification. Documents that have the force of an order are signed where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's just a normal regular order, it's to the right, but if it's sent as a telegram then it's to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies line 63, 3. Okay. Continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, sir, it is both my mistake and yours. Please, can you wait after I put my question to you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- before you respond, and then I will also try to wait. Can you now look at this document to see if the person to whom it is addressed is stated here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is this document sent to any unit of the MUP or the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please look at document P2106? I apologise. P1878. P1878. You commented yesterday on this order during your examination-in-chief. Can you please look at it, especially paragraph 5, and if you can tell me if the tasks issued to any MUP unit are referred to in this order. Can we look at paragraph -- or the part of the document marked with the 5. That's where the tasks are laid out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5.1 is the task to the 125th Motorised Brigade that consists of the 2nd Battalion of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade as a subordinate unit under the direct command of the commander of the 125th Brigade. This is why it's put like this, 125th, and then in brackets 2/58.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And 2/58 is what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2 /58 is also a unit from our brigade, but one battalion is taken out and resubordinated to the 125th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So now you will agree with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is not clear in the transcript, thus my question was whether this 2/58, was this a military unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's an establishment unit classified under R [phoen] of the Pristina Corps, while the 125th Brigade is of a classification replenished with more soldier and senior officer cadre than the 58th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Can we pass to the next page so that we can look at this towards the end. Do you see the second page now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is there a task issued to any MUP unit here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not here. There is only in paragraph 3 where joint coordination is regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But the tasks are not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's go back to Exhibit 1966 now, please. Could you please have a look at this order, too, and tell us whether paragraph 3, the task of the Pristina Corps, and after that paragraph 5, task to the units, were tasks given to the MUP units and these documents or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it on the screen yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Not here. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We're looking at the last page. Does it say who this document was sent to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, when we looked at these documents, you said yesterday that such documents were sent to the army units and to the MUP. General Stefanovic testified here who said that such orders were not sent to the MUP units, that they were sent only to the units of the army of Yugoslavia. Also, the deputy head of the MUP staff testified here, Mr. Mijatovic, who on pages 22196 -- or rather 42196 and 22339 said that up until the resubordination order was issued on the 19th of April, the one that you spoke about, the MUP only received excerpts from maps and in no way any orders from the Pristina Corps. Will you agree with what these two witnesses said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know concerns 1998 when I was responsible. That is to say that excerpts were sent to them from the decisions as a basis for coordination. Without the decision, they had nothing to coordinate. That is to say if they don't have the decision, they don't know what to coordinate, so they had to have that. Now, I cannot say how General Stefanovic organised coordination with them. I didn't even know when he went there. I was not very much involved in the writing of combat documents in 1999. In 1998, I was responsible for these combat documents. For 1999, he was the one, and he knows the best what things were like. So I cannot challenge anything that he said. If he said it was that way, then I assume it was that way. I just know that in 1999, I partly took part in the elaboration of documents. I helped in terms of Grom 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Stefanovic testified about that, too, and you explained that to us earlier on. I assume that there is no need for us to go back to the beginning of the document. It is in front of us on our screens. Is this a computer document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the interview that my colleagues showed you, in paragraph 66 you said when Mr. Coo put this order before you for Rogove, you said that most probably this form was taken out of the computer of the Pristina Corps. Is this a correct reflection of your words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look at that, in what context I spoke, and then I'll answer straight away. Sixty-six you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part it could be put that way, that I can remember that this was discussed. From the point of view of the content involved, it should be this way, that the conversation evolved along these lines. I know for sure that he asked me about this document. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot understand Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I accept this explanation as far as I know. I know when the action was carried out, but I was not very much involved in the document itself. I only know that on the map I saw, perhaps when I came here, I saw what was marked. I remember that very well, that one battalion of this 58th Brigade was marked on the south-west slopes of Pec and that it was under blockade. I know that and that practically they were not engaged anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We only have seven or eight minutes left until the break. Let us try to finish this up. So what you said was correct, that there were such templates or forms in the computer of the Pristina Corps. I do apologise. For the transcript, so it is correct that this kind of template was taken out of the computer of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please allow me to finish my question before answering it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you were in Pristina at the forward command post of the 3rd Army in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this command post, this forward command post of the 3rd Army was near the command post of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a certain period it was. That is to say that I remember well because -- I mean, we had a big problem to establish a command post already in the end of 1998. That is to say we asked the army command to state in writing that they gave approval to the Pristina Corps to have a command post because the existing command post in the village of Lebane in the immediate vicinity of Pristina could not provide normal conditions for functioning, and that is when --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you for a simple reason. We don't need such explanations. You were saying yesterday that reports were being sent, and you said it seemed to you, you weren't sure. It's possible that through the operations centre in Nis you got reports from the Pristina Corps. Now, I would be interested in the following: Do you remember that the practice was when there were no communications, and they were down quite often as we heard, that they were sent via courier?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite possible. That is quite possible. I didn't go into that because I had a man who dealt with this question, the chief of communications, one of the operatives. I didn't go into that particular subject matter, so I may make a mistake if I say anything about this. Quite simply, I was not involved in this, and I did not want to give an answer that I would not be certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: General, I just have one question left -- or, rather, I'm asking you for clarification. A few moments ago, you said to my colleague Mr. Aleksic that you know for sure that as for a plan to expel the Albanian civilian population, that that never existed, and you said in 1998. Do you know whether such a plan existed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never heard of any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. General, just one clarification arising out of that last series of questions. When you went to the 3rd Army, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went to the 3rd Army, as I said yesterday, in the period from approximately the 20th of January until the 20th of February, I did stay in Kosovo to help within the corps command and the forward command post of the 3rd Army in order to carry out some of the regular tasks. In that period, roughly for the most part I was within the Pristina corps. Perhaps I did go away for a day or two briefly, but all of that was very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that I went to Nis, to Nis, in order to take over from General Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. That's what I understood. It was in relation to the question about the delivery of reports, but you've confirmed what I thought. Thank you. We'll take our break at this stage before commencing with the final cross-examination. That's for half an hour this time, General, so could you leave the courtroom, please, with the usher. And we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, perhaps we can clarify how we shall deal with the notes and the amplification of the illegible portions. Can I take it that no Defence counsel wish to add anything to the lines identified by the Prosecution for further exploration?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know for sure that our Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that our Defence hasn't seen those yet. We just got the CD. Probably not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- you don't, obviously, have in mind any portions of the thing that you want to quickly check, whether the Prosecution are asking for them to be amplified or not. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have any plans of doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, one possibility, subject to the willingness of the witness, and it's very much a question of that, is that we ask him simply to write out clearly the passages which are marked and pass it to CLSS for a proper translation rather than deal with it by interpretation as the result of an oral statement. Now, that would seem more satisfactory. It may take a little longer, though, but it is probably a more satisfactory arrangement. Now, unless I hear objection to that, then I will ask Mr. Djakovic if he's willing to do that. If that is done -- sorry, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that is done, for the purposes of entire transparency it would be necessary for the parties, then, to submit a filing agreeing that the freshly translated passages -- this only affects the English version -- the English translation, may either be substituted for the existing one or go into the -- I think better to go into the record along with the existing one, and subject to that the Trial Chamber would accept that as an additional part of that Exhibit P1468. Now, does anyone see any obstacle to that? Thank you. Mr. Djakovic, we're looking for your assistance. The Prosecution have identified in the notes of the -- the notes of the meetings of the so-called Joint Command that you made a number of passages which it's not been possible to translate because they are not clear, and everybody's agreed that we should try and get this cleared up with as little formality as possible. The suggestion that has been made is that if the copy marked with the passages that the Prosecution wish to have clarified is passed to you, you could write out clearly what each passage says. Now, first of all, would you be willing to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Secondly, would you be willing to do it this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's very good of you. Thank you very much. Oh, there is a problem though. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We have no problem. On the contrary. As you know, there are over 1.600 mistakes in the document that we wrote in translation, should it remain in with that many -- that many translations in the document or not. I really don't have a problem with that, but they are mistakes, so it's up to you whether that will be corrected. I mean, I don't want to insist. I don't want to extend the trial. This was written in November, and now it's already May, but you are going to have of an incomplete document, and that worries me because really, every one of the mistakes I pointed out is really there, and it is for you to decide now, and I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since it will be a more complete document, then we can probably worry less. It was our insistence that the Prosecution have identified the passages that seem to them to be the most important. Getting this done at all is a bonus at this stage in the proceedings. I understand there are about 80 of them -- 84. If it turns out -- if it's possible for the communication to be made and it turns out that this can be done quite rapidly, no doubt Mr. Hannis would be happy to submit a supplementary list, but I think we'll do -- try to content ourselves with what's been done. Now, Mr. Djakovic, before you leave here at the end of today's proceedings, you will be given the marked copy of this document, and you will also be given a clear and as clear a copy as we have of the original version so that you've got the best opportunity to write clearly the bits that are perhaps not quite as clear as they might be because of the copying process, handwriting, whatever. There's a number of reasons for it. And once you do this and return it, we shall arrange for the passages that you have written out to be translated into English. So the man to deal with -- the man who will deal with this is the gentleman immediately in front of me. He will relate to you what -- exactly what's required when he hands over the material to you later on this afternoon. This gentleman here, Mr. Haider. Okay? Is there anything -- everything clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The final counsel to cross-examine will be Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before we begin, since I am the Defence attorney of Mr. Sreten Lukic, so we're talking about police matters, I would like to ask you if you not knowing something, if you don't know something, to say so because there's no point in answering if you don't know. You don't have to try to explain something if you don't know. First of all, I would like to ask you if you followed these proceedings over the internet.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to listen to the testimony of Mr. Mijatovic and Mr. Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to stop occasionally. It doesn't mean that I'm not happy with the answer but that we're waiting for the transcript to record what we are saying. I can see on page 43, line 21, today, you mention people with their titles and their last names, but you also refer to Obrad. Who did you mean when you say "Obrad"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obrad Stefanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obrad Stefanovic. When was the last time you saw Mr. Obrad Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four months ago. Approximately, it's been four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. First, I'm going to ask you something about police organisation, legal framework. We're going to go through that very quickly, probably, and then we're going to move to factual matters. Did you have the opportunity to read the Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you read the rules on the organisation of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you read the rules on the systematization of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to read the decision on the formation of the PJP units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at P2113 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is a document that you've already been shown issued by the command of the 125th Motorised Brigade, and the document refers to this document of the Joint Command. In the first paragraph, number 1104 from the 6th of October, 1999. Do you recall being asked about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer? It was not recorded in the transcript. You said --

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm just trying to remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on line 13 it says 6th of October, 1999, and the document itself says 6 July of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were asked, you said that you sent this document marked 1104-6, and you said that probably General Lukic was supposed to see to it that his organs also find out about this document and that this would probably -- was to be done by his assistants. You cannot say with certainty whether Sreten Lukic ever dispatched this document 1104-6 further on to the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you -- are you clear that number 1104-6 was sent to Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have to see the signature part to be able to say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you mean the end of this document or the signature part of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the end of this document. No, no. Actually, the previous one, 1104-6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you expect it to have been sent to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question was answered by the witness yesterday. It's at, I'm sorry, page 75 of yesterday's transcript on line 3. "Did that document number 1104-6 of 6th July also go to the MUP?" The answer: "No, no. There was no need."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We formed the view that the answers were not clear on this subject yesterday, Mr. Ackerman. I see my transcript regrettably has been brought up-to-date, so I don't have the right reference. Oh, no, I may have it. You see, that was an incomplete answer you gave me. It then goes on. "The one from 125th? You mean 1104-6? No, no. There was no need." Now, the 1104-6 was not from the 125th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. That's right, and then he goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is a confusing answer, and that's what I'm trying to clarify now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What our next question was -- I don't mean the one from Zivanovic but the one he received from -- you understand which I understand is, and he said, "I know. It definitely didn't go there because I personally drafted it, and I know it didn't." I don't think there's any inclarity about it at all, but if you want to go back into it, it's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, if you go to line 11, you get reference to Colonel Zivanovic when he showed the document with the words "Joint Command." The MUP received the same document from General Lukic. It's difficult to understand how that would happen without Lukic getting the originating document. So I understand your point on this, but we found the overall situation less than clear. And it's helpful, Mr. Lukic, if you can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard the discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one second because the question I did ask was interrupted, and the question was: Would you expect the document 1104-6 to have been sent to Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would rather be no than yes, and let me explain that briefly. If there is a previous order from the army commander banning the use of the army in specific situations without his knowledge and specifically -- or exclusively for the support of the MUP, so I think that this document 1104-6 was done on the basis of that document of the army commander. So it arises from that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djakovic, you also talked about the implementation of documents and that General Pavkovic and General Lukic actually represented bodies comprising the Joint Command. You say what the two of them would agree would be implemented, and then as you say, not they personally but their assistants in the relevant sectors. So in relation to this, I would ask you this: How many sectors had General Lukic as part of the Kosovo and Metohija staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was directed by him personally to two people for purposes of coordination. I was directed to Mijatovic, and Mijatovic most frequently then sent me to Adamovic. I did have contacts with Mijatovic but very rarely. He would pass me to Adamovic more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know how many men the MUP staff had?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know are the activities that had to do with General Obrad Stefanovic, with Adamovic, and partially to Mijatovic. My affairs with them, I didn't have any contacts with other organs. Mostly my contacts were with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you think that Obrad Stefanovic was a member of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that he had specific authority to deploy and engage the PJP units. I don't know if this authority -- this authorisation came from General Lukic or not, but he gave me elements to engage PJP units in order for them to be technically done in the way that was essential to us so that this decision could be approved by the army commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And now I would like to look at 6D293. We have a lot of documents like this. I'm going to show you one of them. You can see here document from the internal affairs secretariat of Uzice being sent to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, to the police administration, to the PJP command. The document is from the 22nd of March, 1999. Do you know that at the time there was a PJP command? Are you aware of that, and do you know who was in that command?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of the function from what I understood of Obrad Stefanovic, that he was in the police administration, the chief of the police administration. This is what I know purely from some personal contacts. Otherwise, I was never -- I never had the opportunity to see these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the sake of the transcript at page 79, line 15, I believe the witness said in Serbian the word "sef," [phoen] which means chief of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say that, Mr. Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that he was responsible for the police administration. As for the function that he had, as I say, I don't know, but through personal contacts I knew that he was responsible for -- within the framework of the police administration. It's possible that I did say the word "chief."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is not in dispute anyway.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. So unrelated to this document do you know how the planning of regular activities in MUP was conducted? How did that proceed? Annual plans, monthly plans?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I really cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, this is why I said at the beginning if you don't know, yeah, you can just say that since this is not really your area of knowledge. Are you aware and did you read relevant documents so that you would know about the chain of command in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know something about that purely from contacts with people that I had contacts with down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in relation to that, did you know if the MUP staff was an organisational unit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the MUP staff was not an organisational unit. It was not an organisational unit, but anyway, let's move on. Do you know how reporting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The translation -- I think that that answer ended with "I think that it was," and that it was Mr. Lukic who -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now I'd like to ask you whether you know how reporting took place within the MUP directly and the lines of reporting on the sides.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I know from the direct contacts I had with people, from General Lukic, Obrad Stefanovic, Adamovic, Mijatovic, and so on. I know that General Lukic liaised with the secretariats of the interior within the territory of Kosovo. I think there were seven secretariats as far as I can remember. He also had around 24 departments of the interior that relied on these seven secretariats within the municipalities. So it is these seven largest municipalities. I heard that. They had direct communication with the minister of the interior, too. I heard that, as well, and that they reported with regard to certain issues pertaining to their functional tasks, crime traffic, and so on that, that they informed the minister of the interior about that, and that General Lukic communicated with the minister of the interior, a separate line in terms of the tasks that he had received from the minister. That is what I know from the people I contacted with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is more than we expected. Thank you. In respect of reporting, do you know what kind of communications resources the MUP staff had in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, I saw that they had Motorolas. At the command post, General Lukic's once, I happened to see him talking to somebody. Now, was it the secretariat? Was it one of his units? I don't know, but he was talking on a Motorola, that is to say from his command post. And the subordinate units for the most part had Motorolas. I don't know what type. But with regard to communications or signals, rather, I was never really much of an expert, and it's not that I was really that well-versed in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say command post, you're probably referring to the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office, the place where General Lukic commanded and carried out the tasks that he had. For me, that is his command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are a bit in military terms now, but we do understand each other, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what communications resources existed at the MUP staff during 1999, especially after the 29th of March, because you yourself know that the SUP building in Pristina was hit on that day.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There was never any need for me to resolve such matters. Within the command of the Pristina Corps, there was a chief of communications who had contacts with the chief of communications from the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for any command over actions, is it indispensable to have technical resources in order to have communication? Can there be command if there are no technical facilities for having permanent contact with units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it really cannot be done that way. There have to be possibilities for commanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally ever see a written order of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Sreten Lukic? Did he often go out into the field, or was he mostly in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from time to time -- well, he spent more time in Pristina, a lot more time in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, could someone who was not a member of the PJPs command the PJPs? If you can give an answer to this question at all. If you cannot, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We had witnesses here, and I'm not going to go into the actual names and what it was that they were saying and who said what, but we did have witnesses here who were members of the PJP who testified about the command structure of the PJP. Would they be more familiar than you with the command structure of the PJP, that is to say of these units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Kosovo in 1998, you said yourself that Sreten Lukic was there, Obrad Stefanovic, Vlastimir Djordjevic. I apologise for having misspoken. Do you know, first of all, about the relationship between Obrad Stefanovic and Sreten Lukic? Who was whose superior, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have any document, but I know within my own functional duties with who I resolved certain problems. Now, who was subordinated to who, I really don't know, and who had what kind of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You were asked, but I would like to ask you too. Did you directly participate in drafting the plan for combatting terrorism?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for this plan that you wrote up -- or, rather, in whose writing you participated, were the police units envisaged to participate together with the units of the army of Yugoslavia and these anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to skip something. Perhaps we will have to go back but not now, but anyway, 4D495. Could that please be shown to us now. We see a map in front of us. Could it please be zoomed in a bit more. Was this kind of map sent to Dusan Samardzic, army commander, for approval?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the map where the police units are marked and the army and police units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in accordance with how work maps should be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you're a better expert on this than I am, so I'm just seeking further clarification.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you make excerpts of maps from the main maps in view of the units that were on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, excerpts were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you send these excerpts to the units that are marked on the decision map?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Of the MUP. If you mean the MUP. They were sent to the people who were on the MUP staff, and then they further distributed it. Further on, they had some obligations to carry through before sending instructions to their subordinate units. That is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. First of all, I would like us to look at some excerpts from maps for lower-ranking units. First of all, it is 6D1618. While we're waiting for that, you'll see it is about the Cicavica action, and it is the 8th PJP detachment. Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the draftsman who processes documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. This is one of the excerpts that was made and sent through the MUP staff, inter alia, to the PJP units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, who wrote this excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it's the technical draftsman. He is ordered to do this, to make these excerpts for all adjacent units, all the units involved, and this command is supposed to assess the situation and to make decisions and write an order and the decision on the map. So this is just a basis for coordination for the unit to which it is sent. This is not the order itself. It's not the decision, either. This is an excerpt from the decision of the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 6D1620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you to clarify one thing. You said that maps were passed to people on the MUP staff and then they further distributed the extract, and this is how your words have been translated: "Further on, they had some obligations to carry through before sending instructions to their subordinate units." Now, what were these obligations that they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that means that it's part of the obligations that the command or the neighbour, the unit acting in concert, has in respect of the planned coordination. That means that this command, once it receives this extract or excerpt from the decision, not that particular one, but all commands, they have to have a process take place in the commander's head. He should see where the place of his unit is and the role of his unit in view of the tasks to see who is on his right, who is on his left, and on the basis of that, he works out the basic concept or idea for combat documents. That is to say every command, including the MUP command -- or, rather, the MUP detachment, including the combat group, brigade, has to carry out this process. This is a purely professional part, so that ultimately their own decision would be made. So every brigade commander made his own decision on how forces will be used in accordance with the idea of the superior commander. That's the way it is from the general staff down to the company, that is to say the entire process. The detachment command in order to perform with top marks has three or five hours at its disposal. That involves making the decision map and writing the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you're talking in military terminology when you say all this. Are you actually speaking from personal knowledge that that is what would happen in a MUP detachment -- PJP detachment which received the extract?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That has to happen in accordance with the rules. I am talking about military rules. Now, how the MUP regulated this, I never went into that, and the command of the Pristina Corps did not have jurisdiction in terms of having control over the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djakovic. You don't know exactly what all took place at the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have 6D1620 here now. That is a decision on this map, right? Do you know from what year this map is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look at the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can see Kosmac action.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998. 1998. I believe it's 1998 because things were done this way in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And this is the excerpt for the 8th detachment. This is a coded map, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So axis are drawn in on a map that has been coded previously, or is it coded later? How does it happen that we have both on one map? Can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible since after coordination at the level of the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps and the implementation of the duties that we had at our level, the commands would from both sides receive the excerpts, and then based on the excerpts they would organise the joint action along specific axis, which means that the commander of the 8th detachment and the military unit that was supporting the MUP. This would be in the regulations. It's a duty. And without that, the units would not be able to function because they would then fire at each other. So if there was no coordinated action, they would be affected by artillery fire or something like that from the army, so I assume that the commanders in the field probably had the maps -- on their own maps on the decisions agreed how they would communicate in the course of combat in order to keep each other informed if they were not close to each other. If they were near one another, they could agree on the spot if they would stop firing or continue in some other axis or things like that. I simply cannot give you an answer for each individual case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But it says "Coded map Drim." Is that some of usual thing?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. This just applied to this map. You couldn't have several maps with the same name. That was not something that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 6D1619, please. This is a decision on the map. Again, we're talking about Kosmac, but it's an excerpt for the PJPPZ company, Prizren company, so excerpts were done for independent SUP units as well. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was an independent unit at the level of a detachment, and that's why this was done for the PJP police units together with the staff members, since a company was an independent unit at the level of a detachment because there were nine companies within Kosovo. Two municipalities had two each, and seven municipalities had one each, and so this was done the same according to the same principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you said, Mr. Lukic, PJPPZ. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] That's right. It's for Prizren, abbreviation for Prizren.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So now let's just look at 6D1621, please. This is the Drenica sector, and it's an excerpt for the 35th PJP Detachment. Was this drafted at the time when you were in the Pristina Corps? Do you recognise this, or was this drafted in a different way, this map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DJAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. The draftsman is the same. I would have to have the time when the activity was executed. We did have activities in Drenica in 1998, and several times at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's my mistake. I forgot that you are not actually the one that draws the map. Excuse me. Let us now look at P1878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Lukic, we should call it a day at this stage and not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- cause difficulty for the afternoon. As yesterday, Mr. Djakovic, we have to abandon the courtroom to another court -- another case for the afternoon, so if you could please leave the courtroom with the usher. Shortly, the court deputy, Mr. Haider, will be in touch with you and pass to you the documents that we would like you to deal with this afternoon, and please also bear in mind that you do this job in splendid isolation and must not communicate with anybody other, obviously, than court staff for this purpose about the evidence in the case. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we'll see you again here tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
